solutions.17: Continuity at x = 1 requires the left value and right-hand limit to be equal. Thus k + 2 = 1² + 2(1) = 3, so k = 1.
solutions.18: Let u = eˣ. Since d(tan⁻¹u)/dx = u′/(1 + u²), dy/dx = eˣ/(1 + e²ˣ).
solutions.19: Differentiate implicitly: 2x + x(dy/dx) + y + 2y(dy/dx) = 0. Hence dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). At (1, 2), dy/dx = −4/5.
solutions.20: Take logarithms: log y = x log(x² + 1). Differentiating gives (1/y)(dy/dx) = log(x² + 1) + 2x²/(x² + 1). Therefore dy/dx = (x² + 1)ˣ[log(x² + 1) + 2x²/(x² + 1)].
solutions.21: dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ) = (a cos θ)/(−a sin θ) = −cot θ. Therefore d²y/dx² = [d(−cot θ)/dθ]/(dx/dθ) = csc²θ/(−a sin θ) = −1/(a sin³θ).
solutions.22: First, dy/dx = eˣ(sin x + cos x) + eˣ(cos x − sin x) = 2eˣ cos x. Hence d²y/dx² = 2eˣ(cos x − sin x).
solutions.23: For continuity at x = 1, a + b = 1. The left derivative is a and the right derivative of x² at 1 is 2, so a = 2 and b = −1. With these values f is continuous and differentiable. solutions.24: (a) dx/dθ = −4 sin θ. (b) dy/dθ = 3 cos θ. (c) dy/dx = −(3/4)cot θ, so at θ = π/4 the slope is −3/4. Also d²y/dx² = [d(−(3/4)cot θ)/dθ]/(−4 sin θ) = −3/(16 sin³θ). At θ = π/4 this is −3√2/8.

solutions.18: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2). This is positive for x < 0 and x > 2, and negative for 0 < x < 2. Thus f is increasing on (−∞, 0) and (2, ∞), and decreasing on (0, 2).
solutions.19: Let f(x) = x + 4/x. Then f′(x) = 1 − 4/x², so the positive critical point is x = 2. Since f″(x) = 8/x³ > 0, this is a minimum. The minimum value is f(2) = 4.

solutions.18: The circle has radius 4. Its first-quadrant part is one quarter of the circle, so the area is (1/4)π(4)² = 4π square units.
solutions.19: The curves meet where x = x², giving x = 0 and x = 1. On [0, 1], y = x lies above y = x². Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = 1/6 square unit.
solutions.20: The intersections satisfy x² = 2x, so x = 0, 2. On [0, 2], the line is above the parabola. Area = ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3]₀² = 4/3 square units.

solutions.17: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2. The equation is polynomial in its derivatives and the highest-order derivative has power 1, so the degree is 1.
solutions.18: Separate variables: dy/y = 2 dx. Hence log|y| = 2x + C, so y = Ce²ˣ. Since y(0) = 3, C = 3. Therefore y = 3e²ˣ.
solutions.19: Separate variables: (1 + y²)dy = (1 + x²)dx. Integrating gives y + y³/3 = x + x³/3 + C.
solutions.20: Write y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x(dv/dx). The equation becomes v + x(dv/dx) = 1 + v, hence x(dv/dx) = 1. Thus v = log|x| + C. Since v = y/x, the solution is y = x[log|x| + C].
solutions.21: This is linear with integrating factor exp(∫1 dx) = eˣ. Hence d(yeˣ)/dx = xeˣ. Integrating, yeˣ = eˣ(x − 1) + C. Therefore y = x − 1 + Ce⁻ˣ.
solutions.22: Treat x as a function of y. The integrating factor is exp(∫tan y dy) = sec y. Multiplying gives d(x sec y)/dy = tan y. Hence x sec y = ∫tan y dy = log|sec y| + C.
solutions.23: Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x(dv/dx). Then v + x(dv/dx) = (1 + v)/(1 − v), giving (1 − v)/(1 + v²) dv = dx/x. Integration gives tan⁻¹v − (1/2)log(1 + v²) = log|x| + C. With v = y/x, this simplifies to tan⁻¹(y/x) − (1/2)log(x² + y²) = C. The condition (x, y) = (1, 0) gives C = 0. Thus tan⁻¹(y/x) = (1/2)log(x² + y²).
solutions.24: (a) The order is 1 and the degree is 1. (b) The integrating factor is exp(∫(1/2)dt) = exp(t/2). (c) Multiplying by the integrating factor gives d[M exp(t/2)]/dt = 4 exp(t/2). Hence M exp(t/2) = 8 exp(t/2) + C and M = 8 + C exp(−t/2). Since M(0) = 0, C = −8. Therefore M(t) = 8[1 − exp(−t/2)], and M(2) = 8(1 − e⁻¹).

notes.subtitle: Continuity, Composite Rules & Higher Derivatives

concepts.title: Continuity at a point
concepts.text: A function is continuous at x = a when the left-hand limit, right-hand limit and f(a) all exist and are equal. Piecewise functions must be checked at their joining points.

concepts.title: Differentiability and continuity
concepts.text: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there, but continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability. Corners, cusps and vertical tangents require special care.

concepts.title: Composite and implicit functions
concepts.text: Use the chain rule from the outer function inward. For an implicit relation, differentiate every term with respect to x and collect the terms containing dy/dx.

concepts.title: Special derivative forms
concepts.text: Logarithmic differentiation is efficient for variable powers and products. Parametric derivatives use dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), and the same idea gives the second derivative.

formulas: Continuity at a: lim x→a⁻ f(x) = lim x→a⁺ f(x) = f(a)
d[f(g(x))]/dx = f′(g(x))g′(x)
d(sin⁻¹x)/dx = 1/√(1 − x²)
d(cos⁻¹x)/dx = −1/√(1 − x²)
d(tan⁻¹x)/dx = 1/(1 + x²)
d(eᵘ)/dx = eᵘ du/dx; d(log u)/dx = (1/u)du/dx
For x > 0, d(xˣ)/dx = xˣ(1 + log x)
For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
d²y/dx² = [d(dy/dx)/dt]/(dx/dt)
method: For continuity, check only the points where the defining expression changes or may be undefined.
Identify whether the function is composite, implicit, logarithmic or parametric before differentiating.
Apply the relevant rule one layer at a time and keep every chain-rule factor.
Simplify the result and, for a second derivative, differentiate the complete first derivative again.

example.question: If x = a cos θ and y = a sin θ, find d²y/dx².
steps: First find dy/dx = (a cos θ)/(−a sin θ) = −cot θ.
Differentiate −cot θ with respect to θ to obtain csc²θ.

practice.question: Find k if f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = x² + 1 for x > 1 is continuous at 1.
Differentiate sin⁻¹(3x).
If x² + y² = 10, find dy/dx.
Differentiate y = (1 + x²)ˣ logarithmically.
If x = t² and y = t³, find d²y/dx² for t ≠ 0.
If y = eˣ sin x, find d²y/dx².

tips: A continuous function can still fail to be differentiable.
When differentiating implicitly, dy/dx accompanies every derivative involving y.
Inverse-trigonometric derivatives need both the correct sign and the chain-rule factor.
For parametric second derivatives, divide the derivative of dy/dx by dx/dt; do not merely differentiate with respect to t.

notes.subtitle: Rates, Monotonicity & Optimisation

concepts.title: Related rates
concepts.text: Express the quantities in one equation, differentiate with respect to time, and substitute the values only after differentiation.

concepts.title: Increasing and decreasing
concepts.text: On an interval, f′(x) > 0 indicates increase and f′(x) < 0 indicates decrease. Critical numbers divide the domain into sign-test intervals.

concepts.title: Local extrema
concepts.text: A change of f′ from positive to negative gives a local maximum; a change from negative to positive gives a local minimum.

concepts.title: Absolute extrema and modelling
concepts.text: On a closed interval compare critical points and endpoints. In a word problem, define the variable and its feasible domain before maximising or minimising.

formulas: If f′(x) > 0 on an interval, f is increasing there
If f′(x) < 0 on an interval, f is decreasing there
If f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) < 0, f has a local maximum at a
If f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) > 0, f has a local minimum at a
Circle: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, so dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt
Cylinder: V = πr²h
Rectangle with perimeter 2p: A = x(p − x)
method: Define the changing or decision variable and write its valid domain.
Rewrite the required quantity as a function of one variable whenever optimising.
Differentiate, locate critical points, and make a sign table or use the second-derivative test.
Check endpoints when relevant and state the final answer with units and context.

example.question: A rectangle has perimeter 40 m. Find its maximum area.
steps: Let the sides be x and 20 − x, so A = x(20 − x).
A′ = 20 − 2x, which is zero at x = 10.
A″ = −2 < 0, so this critical point gives a maximum.
example.answer: The rectangle is 10 m by 10 m and its maximum area is 100 m².

practice.question: The radius of a circle grows at 1 cm/s. Find dA/dt when r = 4 cm.
Find where f(x) = x² − 4x is increasing.
Find the local extrema of f(x) = x³ − 3x.
practice.answer: Local maximum 2 at x = −1; local minimum −2 at x = 1

practice.question: Find the minimum value of x + 9/x for x > 0.
Two positive numbers have sum 30. Find their maximum product.
Find the absolute maximum and minimum of x² − 2x + 3 on [0, 4].
practice.answer: Minimum 2 at x = 1; maximum 11 at x = 4

tips: In related rates, differentiate before inserting the numerical instant.
A critical point need not be an extremum; test the derivative sign or second derivative.
The second-derivative test is inconclusive when f″(a) = 0.
A closed-interval absolute extremum may occur at an endpoint.

notes.subtitle: Areas Under and Between Standard Curves

concepts.title: Geometric area
concepts.text: A definite integral is signed, but geometric area is non-negative. Split the interval wherever a curve crosses the axis or the upper and lower boundaries change.

concepts.title: Vertical strips
concepts.text: When boundaries are naturally y = f(x), integrate upper curve minus lower curve with respect to x.

concepts.title: Horizontal strips
concepts.text: When boundaries are naturally x = g(y), integrate right curve minus left curve with respect to y.

concepts.title: Standard conics
concepts.text: Use symmetry for circles, ellipses and parabolas, but still find the exact intersection points that bound the required region.

formulas: Area under y = f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b]: A = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx
Area between curves: A = ∫ₐᵇ [upper − lower] dx
Horizontal-strip area: A = ∫_c^d [right − left] dy
Circle x² + y² = a²: area = πa²
Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: area = πab
Parabola y² = 4ax: x = y²/(4a)
Parabola x² = 4ay: y = x²/(4a)
method: Sketch both boundaries and shade the required region.
Solve the boundary equations together to find all intersection points.
Choose vertical or horizontal strips so that the limits and boundary functions stay simple.
Integrate the positive width or height, splitting the region when a boundary changes.

example.question: Find the area enclosed by y = x and y = x².
steps: Solve x = x² to obtain x = 0 and x = 1.
On [0, 1], y = x is above y = x².
example.answer: The enclosed area is 1/6 square unit.

practice.question: Find the area under y = 3x from x = 0 to x = 2.
Find the area of a quadrant of the circle x² + y² = 25.
Find the area enclosed by y = x and y = x².
Find the area enclosed by y = 2x and y = x².
Find the area bounded by y = x² and y = 9.
Find the first-quadrant area of x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.

tips: Geometric area uses positive strip lengths, not an unexamined signed integral.
For side-opening parabolas, integrating with respect to y is often shorter.
Use symmetry only after confirming that both the curve and required region are symmetric.

notes.subtitle: Classification, Separation, Homogeneous & Linear Forms

concepts.title: Order, degree and solutions
concepts.text: Order is the order of the highest derivative. Degree is the power of that derivative after the equation is polynomial in derivatives. A general solution contains the appropriate arbitrary constant; an initial condition selects a particular solution.

concepts.title: Separation of variables
concepts.text: Rewrite the equation so that all y terms multiply dy and all x terms multiply dx, then integrate both sides.

concepts.title: Homogeneous first-order equations
concepts.text: If dy/dx is a function of y/x, put y = vx. Then dy/dx = v + x(dv/dx), producing a separable equation in v and x.

concepts.title: Linear first-order equations
concepts.text: Write the equation as dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), multiply by its integrating factor, and recognise the left side as the derivative of a product. The corresponding x-as-a-function-of-y form is treated similarly.

formulas: General first-order linear form: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x)
Integrating factor = exp(∫P(x) dx)
After multiplying: d[y·IF]/dx = Q(x)·IF
Linear form in x: dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y)
For a homogeneous equation, y = vx and dy/dx = v + x(dv/dx)
If dy/dx = g(x)h(y), then dy/h(y) = g(x)dx
The general solution of dy/dx = ky is y = Ceᵏˣ
method: Identify the order, degree and structural type before solving.
Use separation when x and y factors can be placed on opposite sides.
For a homogeneous right-hand side, substitute y = vx and then separate v and x.
For a linear equation, standardise the coefficient of the first derivative, find the integrating factor, integrate, and apply any initial condition.

example.question: Solve dy/dx + y = x.
steps: Here P(x) = 1, so the integrating factor is eˣ.

practice.question: Find the order and degree of (d²y/dx²)³ + dy/dx = 0.
Solve dy/dx = 4y.
Solve y(dy/dx) = x.
Solve dy/dx = 1 + y/x.
Solve dy/dx + 2y = eˣ.
Solve dx/dy + x = y.

tips: Degree is defined only after radicals or fractions involving derivatives have been removed and the equation is polynomial in derivatives.
Do not confuse a homogeneous differential equation with a homogeneous linear equation.
Include the arbitrary constant only once in a general solution.
For dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y), the integrating factor is a function of y.
